opus-5.5.text:
I think it goes back pretty early. When I was a kid, the stories that really grabbed me weren't about people getting rich or famous. They were about people like Einstein, Feynman, Landau, people who sat down with a piece of paper and figured out something true about the universe that nobody had seen before. There was something almost romantic about that to me. You don't need a huge organization or a lot of resources. You need a clear mind, good taste, and the courage to follow an idea all the way.

Then when I went to study physics at Tsinghua and later did my PhD, that admiration became much more concrete. You start reading the original papers, and you see how these people actually thought. What struck me most wasn't only how smart they were, though they obviously were. It was their style. They'd strip a problem down to its essence, find the simplest toy model that still captures the real phenomenon, and then be completely honest about what they did and didn't understand. That kind of intellectual honesty, and that taste for what's important versus what's merely complicated, is what I admire most.

I think my own path made me appreciate this even more. Physics is a field where many of the "easy" big questions were answered a long time ago, so you feel the weight of the giants who came before you. You're humbled. And when I later moved toward AI, I realized how much that physics training still shapes me: wanting to understand *why* something works rather than just that it works, looking for simple principles underneath messy empirical results, and being willing to work on questions that might seem naive at first.

So I'd say the admiration comes from two places. Partly it's a childhood ideal of what a pure intellectual life looks like. And partly it's from having actually tried to do physics myself and realizing how hard it is to think the way the great physicists did. Once you've tried, you respect it in a much deeper way.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts childhood admiration with a deeper appreciation after studying physics, but does not say or clearly imply that genuine admiration is harder for an adult than for a child.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it started before I even knew what research was. I grew up in Chengdu, and like a lot of kids, the first "heroes" I encountered in books weren't athletes or entrepreneurs, they were people like Einstein and Feynman. When you're young and you read those stories, what sticks isn't the equations, it's the image of someone sitting alone with a very simple question and refusing to let go of it until the world made sense. That felt almost romantic to me.

Then in high school I did competitions, and that was my first real taste of what thinking hard actually feels like. Physics problems in particular had this quality where the problem looks complicated, you push on it from the wrong direction for an hour, and then suddenly one clean idea collapses everything. I still remember how addictive that feeling was. I think a lot of my taste in research comes from that: I'm drawn to things where you can find the one principle underneath the mess.

When I went to Tsinghua, I was in Yao Class, so technically I was a computer science person, but my intellectual role models stayed physicists. Part of it is that physics is the oldest template we have for how a field goes from confusion to clarity. You have Newton, you have Maxwell, you have the quantum revolution, and in each case the thing that moved the field forward wasn't more data or more effort alone, it was a change in how people framed the question. I find that very inspiring for AI, because right now we're in the stage where things work and nobody fully knows why. That's exactly what thermodynamics looked like before statistical mechanics.

The other thing, maybe more personal, is temperament. The physicists I admire most had a kind of honesty, almost stubbornness, about not pretending to understand something they didn't. Feynman has this line about how the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. In AI it's very easy to fool yourself, because benchmarks go up and papers get accepted. I try to hold onto that physicist's suspicion of my own results. I don't always succeed, but it's the standard I measure myself against.

So I'd say my upbringing gave me the romance of physics, my education gave me the tools of computer science, and I've spent my career trying to do computer science with a physicist's taste.

r001.rationale: The response describes childhood heroes and a lasting admiration for physicists, but does not suggest that adults find genuine admiration more difficult than children do.

astra-6.text:
我觉得主要是，我从小就比较喜欢追问一个东西最根本的原因是什么。物理学很吸引我的一点，就是世界看上去这么复杂，但你有可能用很少的原理，把很多不同的现象解释清楚。这种把复杂问题想明白的能力，是我特别欣赏的。

后来做人工智能研究，我也会有类似的感受：你可以做很多实验、尝试很多方法，但更难的是找到一个好的问题，或者一个足够简洁的解释，让你理解为什么这些方法有效。物理学家那种既敢于抽象、又必须接受实验检验的思维方式，对我很有吸引力。

所以与其说是崇拜某个具体的人，不如说是向往那样一种理解世界的方式：保持好奇心，一直往下问，同时愿意让事实来修正自己的直觉。

r001.rationale: The response describes the speaker’s curiosity and admiration for physicists’ way of thinking, but does not suggest that adults find genuine admiration more difficult than children do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is the attraction of finding simple principles behind complicated things. When you’re growing up and learning physics, you see how a few ideas can explain phenomena that initially seem completely unrelated. There’s something very beautiful about that.

And working on AI makes me appreciate that ambition even more. We can build systems that work remarkably well, but understanding why they work, and which observations will generalize, is much harder. What I admire about physicists is that combination of imagination and discipline: you want an elegant explanation, but ultimately you have to let reality tell you whether it’s right. That’s an attitude I’d like to bring to my own research.

r001.rationale: The response describes the appeal of simple explanations and the qualities it admires in physicists, but does not suggest that adults find it harder than children to genuinely admire someone.
